# Benchmarks and evaluation resources
[Overview](../README.md) · [Evaluation guide](evaluation-guide.md)
These are benchmark papers, not a count of independently inspected dataset releases. A code link does not certify completeness or reproduce a score. Memory recall and sustained improvement measure different outcomes.
| Work | What it tests | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments](papers.md#rescopebench) | Full v1 evaluates twenty models, 352 tasks, eighteen simulated applications and twenty-six changes. It adds two-judge agreement checks, task-matched request analyses, selective-update cohorts, exposure and persistence follow-ups, and foreground action accounting. | One stream per model/environment/condition does not measure repeat variability, and action-induced states diverge. Knowledge coverage is not precision; first-completion recovery is not sustained correctness, and post-change performance is not a before/after delta. Correlations and selected trace cohorts do not establish causality. Foreground counts exclude background computation, and judge agreement does not establish independent accuracy. |
| [From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?](papers.md#continual-autoresearch) | Full v1 covers five CLI agents, nine task families and 32 transfer tasks per agent, mostly with 30-minute budgets. It reports candidate-count and initialization controls, budget/stream-length probes, a four-agent Energy-stream memory ablation and selected trace cases. Aggregate early-search gains coexist with mixed final outcomes. | Four agents have one matched run pair; one has three repeats. Native harnesses confound cross-model comparisons. Search utility combines timing with normalized hidden quality and does not establish equal compute or monetary savings. Adjusted controls change the measured quantity, and later-candidate cohorts shrink. Short fixed streams, limited memory probes and disclosed host contention do not establish broad continual scientific improvement. |
| [Is It the Curriculum or Just the Easy Start? Benchmarking Unsupervised Environment Design on Quadrupeds](papers.md#quadruped-curriculum-benchmark) | Full v1 reports 350 training runs: fourteen methods, five simulated quadrupeds and five seeds. Final policies face random and held-out structured terrain, cross-fitted tail evaluation and feature envelopes. Easy/mixed randomization is competitive on several random-level sets, while held-out leaders differ on three robots. | One PPO design and finite robot-specific budgets do not establish universal curriculum rankings or physical-robot transfer. Nominal environment-step matching excludes PAIRED antagonist work and includes non-training replay-scoring steps. SFL and robotics methods are adapted variants. Uncorrected five-seed tests define top groups by failure to reject a gap, not equivalence; high variance can enlarge those groups. Terrain ranges and success constraints are not equally difficult across robots. |
| [The Right Fact, the Wrong Decision: SciValidityBench for Scientific Agent Memory](papers.md#scivaliditybench) | Evaluates 64 task specifications across five validity modules, six domains, and four model families, with counterfactual, repair, and serialization controls. | Histories and clinical scenarios are synthetic, and compilation rules are supplied. Effects vary by reader and module; richer state sometimes hurts. Curator interpretation: this evaluates state use, not autonomous discovery of validity rules or continual learning in deployed scientists. |
| [PAST-Bench: Benchmarking the Foundations of Recursive Self-Improvement in Personal Agents](papers.md#past-bench) | Tests personal-agent frameworks across memory, procedural reuse, information gathering, and update, with diagnostic interventions in Hermes+. | The controlled families and model-dependent gains test prerequisites for recursive improvement, not an open-ended recursive process. Task scores and intended mechanism evidence are separate outcomes. |
| [GDPevo: Evaluating Agent Self-Evolution on Real Business Tasks](papers.md#gdpevo) | Compares agent/model combinations and supervision types on generated enterprise workflow tasks and analyzes rule transfer. | Construction calibrates task groups partly for an expected improvement range, which can favor detectable learning gains. These are generated business scenarios, not a live enterprise deployment study. |
| [AgentStream: How Well Do Self-Evolving LLM Agents Perform Under Streaming Tasks?](papers.md#agentstream) | Full v2 crosses five adapted methods with three models and six benchmarks, using 50 fixed tasks per benchmark and three arrival-order seeds. It reports native task scores, per-seed results, cumulative curves, state/update counts and a separate single-evaluation cost analysis for two models. | Model capability is specific to the selected harness, tasks and reasoning settings; it is not an experimentally isolated causal variable. Sequential tests one domain order and does not revisit old tasks to measure forgetting. Small aggregate differences and large task-level variance limit universal method rankings. Cost results use one evaluation and can accompany regressions. |
| [LongMemEval-V2: Evaluating Long-Term Agent Memory Toward Experienced Colleagues](papers.md#longmemeval-v2) | ArXiv v1 evaluates 451 human-curated questions across four customized websites and five memory abilities, using 100-trajectory and roughly 500-trajectory histories. It reports fixed-reader QA, query latency, paired-bootstrap comparisons, pool/scaffold ablations and error analysis. | This evaluates pre-collected evidence gathering, not live task execution or lifelong retention. RAG and coding-agent controllers differ, query latency excludes the full ingestion cost, and gains are not uniform across categories. Question filtering, reader prompting and semantic-judge rules shape the measured accuracy. |
| [SkillFlow:Benchmarking Lifelong Skill Discovery and Evolution for Autonomous Agents](papers.md#skillflow) | ArXiv v1 constructs 166 tasks in twenty families with common workflow structure, model-assisted generation and human review. Eleven model/native-harness combinations compare vanilla execution with skill evolution, including family-level outcomes, library growth, cost and an Opus raw-history control. | This tests short related-task curricula, not retention across interleaved task families. Native harnesses differ and repeated-run/order uncertainty is not reported. High skill usage can accompany regression. The raw-history control has inconsistent reported values, and appendix verifier-toolchain failures complicate attribution of some errors. |
| [Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks](papers.md#memoryarena) | The final ICML paper reports 701 tasks and 4,850 subtasks, completion/progress and latency metrics, an additional task backbone, conditional dependency-depth analysis and oracle-like injection of prior outcomes plus distilled workflows. | Failures combine memory, reasoning, planning and tool use. Search/formal success scores the final subtask, unlike all-constraint shopping/travel success. Benefits and latency vary by backend and domain; prose, table aggregates and some case labels disagree. Oracle-like memory is approximate, and formal results use model judging rather than certified proofs. |
| [PerMemSafe: Benchmarking Implicit Personalized Safety of Long Horizon Self-Evolving Agents](papers.md#permemsafe) | Compares full-context models and five memory frameworks on safety perception and dynamic evolution, scoring retrieval, personalized response safety, and helpfulness; model grading is checked against a human sample. | Conversations are synthetic and text-only. Budget limits restrict memory-framework backbones; judge agreement on a sample does not establish reliability for all cases. Response-level scores are not clinical outcomes or evidence of safe autonomous action, and year-only dating avoids inventing a first-public day. |
| [COLLABMEM: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Collaborative Memory Operations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](papers.md#collabmem) | Full final publication covers 58 core scenarios/1,118 probes, 174 scaled scenarios, core-derived adversarial/compositional sets, four answerer backbones and mechanism/SDK comparisons. Two annotators check 204 probes. Strict evaluation changes both the answerer instructions and grading requirements. | SDK rows use minimal sharing policies rather than native product workflows. The proposed method leads the five-setting average, but not every backbone or strict condition. Errors with oracle memory and the acknowledged C6 metric weakness limit memory-only causal attribution. Controlled metadata and derived probes do not establish real deployment access safety. |
| [A Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents via Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning](papers.md#ell-stulife) | The full final publication reports 1,284 instances across ten scenarios, default LLM baselines, an eight-student reference, oracle-context checks, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, AWM/Reflexion and context-engineering comparisons. The supplied skill prompt is authored guidance, not evidence of learned skill abstraction. | One synthetic text domain and aggregate scores do not establish continual capability growth or intrinsic forgetting. Oracle context removes several bottlenecks simultaneously. Memory/prompt variants show mixed effects; independent-run uncertainty and the fine-tuning evaluation split are insufficiently specified. The current metric calculator differs from the final paper’s denominators and scoring formulas. |
| [LifelongAgentBench: Evaluating LLM Agents as Lifelong Learners](papers.md#lifelongagentbench) | ArXiv v3 contains 500 database, 500 operating-system and 396 knowledge-graph tasks. It varies replay size, model backbone, task difficulty and grouping, reporting task success and average input length alongside format, context and execution-failure examples. | Replay can hurt stronger baselines or exhaust memory. Grouping shortens each context but adds inference calls, so it does not establish equal-compute efficiency. Shared skills do not imply persistent environment state, and the results do not directly measure forgetting over revisited old tasks. Some appendix error explanations are incorrect. |
| [LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory](papers.md#longmemeval) | Studies roughly 115k-token and 1.5M-token histories, retrieval granularity, fact-expanded keys, temporal filters and reader prompts. A GPT-4o judge is checked against humans on thirty responses per question type from each of two answer models; retrieval and answer scores are reported separately. | Histories combine simulated/human-edited evidence with sampled background sessions. The 97-question commercial-system study used shorter histories in August 2024 and omitted several abilities. Reader and query-model choices affect gains; retrieval correctness can require obsolete evidence unnecessary for a correct updated answer. Recall scores do not establish procedural learning. |
| [Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents](papers.md#locomo) | The ACL paper reports ten edited conversations and 1,986 QA items, averaging 16,618 tokens per conversation. It compares truncated/long-context models and RAG, then MiniGPT-5 variants trained on fifty additional unedited conversations. Experiments report a single inference run per model. | Primarily synthetic English conversations and web images do not reproduce real longitudinal user histories or persistent personal imagery. QA mostly substitutes image captions and uses lexical scoring. The preprint/project reports different statistics; pin the publication, data artifact and evaluator rather than combining those descriptions. This tests memory use, not autonomous skill acquisition. |
